content:
Earlier this year, I replaced my battery-powered lawn mower with an iPhone-controlled robotic mower. You need to manually drive the machine around the perimeter of your yard, and it builds a virtual map. Once setup is complete, it handles mowing automatically on a preset schedule.

Recently, I have been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation approach, and after several weeks of testing, I think it may be a more convenient and easier-to-use option for many people.

Camera-based automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier is how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. Setup required me to manually drive the mower around the boundary with my phone to build the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses what the manufacturer calls a TerraVision 2.0 system. Three cameras let the mower automatically map the lawn area, with no need to lay underground boundary wires or install a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic method of building the initial map clearly takes longer. But I think for people who are not very tech-savvy, this approach may be simpler.

To test this idea, I had my mom, who lives in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without my help. She replied that everything worked fine. I had serious doubts about whether she would have the patience to manually drive the robot around the boundary and manually mark areas to avoid.

Auto-mapping did cause one small oddity in my front yard. Because there is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbor's grass, TerraMow initially included part of the neighbor's lawn in my map.

I fixed it by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, if there is no clear visual boundary between lawns, you will need to pay extra attention during the initial mapping.

Seeing the world through the mower's camera

The camera on the TerraMow also enables one of my favorite features. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to open this view in a large window. I could work indoors while watching the mower navigate the backyard from its perspective.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting, and it can occasionally help explain why it slows down or avoids certain things. The Anthbot M9 has no similar camera-view feature.

The two iPhone apps are quite similar in other respects. Both let you schedule jobs, adjust mowing modes, set zones, mark no-go areas, and remote-control the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly well-designed feature in that last function. Besides traditional left/right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with the iPhone isn't the primary purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should follow the schedule and require no manual input. Still, TerraMow's joystick is very handy for cleaning up missed patches.

Sometimes, it almost feels like I'm controlling the robot with my mind (and it's a pleasant feeling). I can hold the iPhone at my side, give small thumb movements, and the machine moves in the direction I want.

Every robotic mower app should copy this control scheme.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and produced more noise while operating.

I wouldn't call TerraMow loud. It's just that the difference between the two is very obvious. The Anthbot can run so quietly that it's easy to forget it's still there, even when it continues mowing after sunset using its headlight.

Because TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. This makes scheduling it during the day more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and sturdy. It is also bigger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage with the product that covers the charging dock, whereas Anthbot's garage is sold separately.

Most importantly, TerraMow performed reliably. I relied on it for several straight weeks without having to do any of the typical mowing work myself.

When smart mapping becomes too smart

The visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up occasionally backfires.

The mower constantly adjusts its map based on what it sees. Saving these changes after each job takes some time, during which you can't do anything else in the app.

After several days of rain in a row, I ran into an interesting edge case. Part of the yard had standing water, and TerraMow cleverly avoided that area on its next run.

The grass inside the skipped circular patch grew longer. Over time, the mower seemed to interpret this growth as something to keep avoiding, and that patch of grass was never cut again even after the water on the ground had dried up.

I used the app's remote-control function to manually drive the mower through the taller grass, and the problem was resolved. Once that patch returned to the look of a normal lawn, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regularly trimming the edges also helps TerraMow handle boundary areas with confidence. Tall grass growing along unclear boundaries might otherwise be mistaken for obstacles and excluded from the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on boundaries and obstacles you define yourself. That method requires more upfront work, but it also avoids situations where the map changes its mind about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac Review

After using both systems, I lean toward recommending the TerraMow camera approach for most people.

For me, underground boundary wires are a non-starter, and installing an RTK base station means one more piece of hardware to place, power, and maintain. TerraMow requires neither.

Its vision-based navigation isn't perfect. Initial mapping takes longer, invisible boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behavior once mistook overgrown grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In exchange, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, compelling live camera views, and the best manual-control experience I've seen on any robotic mower app.

I actually enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. After handing this task off to a robot, I can spend more time on landscaping, trimming edges, and detailed tidying while keeping the lawn looking neat.

The TerraMow V1000 does well enough at this for me to recommend it, especially for anyone who wants a robotic mower but doesn't want to dig a trench to hide wires, set up an RTK antenna, or walk the entire yard perimeter with a phone.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently available on Amazon and on the official website at US$999 after applying a US$200 coupon. You can also buy it from TerraMow's official site.
